For the displayed recursive construction, ε_{j+1}=C ε_j^{3/2}, L_{j+1}=5L_j, with fixed base net. Thus explicit word length O(log^{log_{3/2}5}(1/ε))=O(log^{3.97}(1/ε)); pointer/DAG compilation time O(log^{log_{3/2}3}(1/ε))=O(log^{2.71}(1/ε)), explicit list time is Ω(output length).

topics_and_locators: Exact QSD synthesizes arbitrary n-qubit U with no ancillas using at most (23/48)4^n−(3/2)2^n+4/3 CNOT gates; the input is an exact abstract unitary matrix and CNOT count is the resource.

The paper reports the generic no-ancilla CNOT lower bound ceil((4^n−3n−1)/4), inherited from dimension counting; it is generic (almost all unitaries), not a per-instance lower bound. Its local proof route should be made explicit as a dimension/parameter-count lemma.

Arbitrary n-qubit state preparation uses at most 2^{n+1}−2n CNOTs. Nearest-neighbor restriction gives at most 9-fold CNOT-count increase in the multiplexed-rotation construction. No numerical-angle bit complexity for computing the QSD decomposition is claimed.

topics_and_locators: Promise problems are disjoint YES/NO sets with arbitrary off-promise behavior. Quantum circuits are encoded as full binary descriptions, and a family is polynomial-time-generated when a deterministic polytime machine emits each circuit description.

BQP(a,b) uses a polytime-generated family with n input qubits and one output qubit, measured in the standard basis; standard BQP is thresholds 2/3 and 1/3. Error robustness is stated for polynomial-time-computable a,b with inverse-polynomial gap.
Proposition 3 states repeated-run error reduction but gives only a short standard-proof sketch; report a separate local majority algorithm and Chernoff/Hoeffding correctness proof.
The paper expressly says the classical depth-space correspondence is not known to transfer in the reverse direction for quantum circuits; it does not prove BQP differs from BPP.

supported_claims_so_far.claim: The course treats the 3-bit repetition code with independent BSC errors; states, without proof, a Shannon-capacity-style existence claim for good classical codes; gives the Shor 9-qubit code, single-qubit Pauli and arbitrary one-qubit unitary error discussions, and a depolarizing noise example; defines binary linear-code distance, duals, generator/parity-check matrices and syndromes; constructs and decodes the Steane CSS code; then states that a positive CSS threshold exists and gives only a rough statement and narrative sketch of the fault-tolerance threshold theorem.

The course develops density matrices, Kraus measurements/channels, Stinespring representations, trace distance and state discrimination. For the assigned scope it does not state or prove the full Knill–Laflamme criterion/recovery theorem, subsystem correction theorem, or an explicit circuit-level threshold model and construction.

The Steane/CSS proof route uses binary linear subspaces C0⊊C1 with C0-perp⊆C1, k=dim(C1)-dim(C0), classical Hamming distance and parity-check syndromes, uniform coset superpositions as logical basis states, Hadamard duality of subspace superpositions, and separate X/Z syndrome extraction; Y errors are handled as iXZ. It does not supply a stabilizer formalism or a general encoding/correcting theorem.

The threshold theorem is explicitly labelled a rough statement: a per-gate/per-time-step precision below some positive constant permits arbitrarily large computations. The course gives no noise independence/locality/correlation model, malignant-location combinatorics, fault-tolerant gadget definitions or proof, concatenation recursion, level-overhead derivation, or threshold constant analysis. These are established-result authoring obligations requiring complete proof suppliers, not open problems.

supported_claims.claim: Defines iid gate/qubit fault locations, sparse fault paths, located-error deviation, bounded-spread quantum computation codes and one-level effective-fault counting.

supported_claims.locator: §4.1 and Appendix C, PDF pp. 8–15; Theorem 2, printed pp. 9 and 11
supported_claims.claim: Proves a concatenated threshold conditional on a fixed-size proper code. For integer q≥1 with 2qℓ≤d, A=binom(a,q+1), where d is correctable located errors, ℓ procedure spread and a an upper bound on base fault locations per rectangle; with iid per-location rate η and Aη^q<1, p0=η and p_(r+1)≤A p_r^(q+1), hence p_r≤A^(−1/q)(A^(1/q)η)^((q+1)^r). Union bound over N output rectangles yields target accuracy δ at r=O(log log(N/δ)) and polylogarithmic overhead for a fixed finite code.

Gives CSS/linear-code examples over F_p and proper-code gadget blueprints; some universal-gate/procedure claims refer to Shor and other sources, so explicit proper-code instantiation needs local proof obligations.

source_limits: Paper’s printed threshold condition uses binom(a,d/(2ℓ)+1)η^(d/(2ℓ))<1; Appendix C writes binom(a,d/(2ℓ)+1)η^(d/(2ℓ)+1)=η^(1+ε). State integer q=floor(d/(2ℓ)) and Aη^q<1 locally to make the contraction exact.
Paper’s d=1 branch is described as “almost the same”; this report uses q≥1 (d≥2ℓ).
The optional locally-stochastic correlated-fault extension is reported separately; the theorem branch uses fully explicit independent fault locations.

supported_claims.claim: The preliminaries distinguish quantum data, finite circuits, universal gate sets, reversible computation, uniformity, quantum complexity, and fault tolerance. §1.4 gives compute-copy-uncompute and warns that mapping a basis state to f(x) is not automatically implementable as a unitary. §1.5 requires an effective circuit generator; §1.6 separates gate size, depth, bounded success, and query complexity. §1.7 only points to a threshold theorem and says the course assumes ideal fault tolerance thereafter.

The notes prove linear operator-norm accumulation under composition and give a Solovay–Kitaev proof route for fixed finite universal gate sets closed under inverses, with a classical synthesis procedure and logarithmic precision overhead.
The notes give exact Clifford+T normal forms and an algebraic characterization; arbitrary-gate approximation requires a separate rounding procedure and is not exact universality of Clifford+T.

The phase-estimation problem is given U as either an explicit circuit or a black box permitting controlled-U^j for integer j, and gives an eigenvector promise. The circuit’s controlled-power access is part of the stated input model.

The course treats query complexity, polynomial and adversary methods, span programs, learning graphs, and compressed oracles. These are query-model results and do not by themselves imply gate-complexity lower bounds for explicit circuits.

Hamiltonian simulation is finite-matrix evolution under explicit decomposition/sparse-access assumptions. Chapter 29 defines a block encoding as an ancilla-zero matrix block, discusses normalization by alpha, uses U and U-dagger plus controlled-U for polynomial transforms, and notes that technical tail estimates are omitted in the final simulation discussion.

The adiabatic theorem and applications assume an initial easily prepared ground state and analyze spectral-gap/evolution conditions; this is not a generic classical-data state-preparation interface or a free data-loading result.

limitations: The author's preface calls the notes rough and invites corrections.
Some advanced technical error estimates and constructions are omitted or cited, so local QC proof obligations remain.
The notes do not provide a complete QC18–QC21 coding and threshold proof route.

supported_claims.claim: Finite-dimensional state vectors, computational-basis measurement, unitary gates, controlled gates and teleportation are introduced. Global phase is invisible in an uncontrolled measurement distribution.

The circuit model distinguishes classical and quantum circuits, gate universality, reversible computation and black-box queries. The bit-flip oracle is the reversible XOR map; a phase oracle is derived by phase kickback with a target eigenstate. Circuit inversion reverses gate order and inverts each gate.
The QFT and phase-estimation construction uses controlled powers and finite output measurement; approximation and output probability are analyzed separately.
Grover search is analyzed by rotations in a two-dimensional invariant subspace; amplitude amplification is stated in terms of a supplied preparation procedure and its reflection/inverse structure.

A finite Hermitian matrix H defines matrix evolution e^{-itH}; simulation uses operator-norm error, with a separate clean-ancilla restricted action metric when the circuit has extra workspace. Sparse input requires explicit value and location oracles and their inverses. Block encoding is an ancilla-zero block, and a sparse-matrix construction consumes those access oracles.

HHL's input contract explicitly includes a circuit of B two-qubit gates preparing the input vector as a quantum state, sparse matrix access, and a condition-number bound. The output is an approximate normalized solution state, not the classical amplitude list.
Polynomial and adversary methods are query-complexity techniques whose inputs and lower bounds depend on the specified oracle model.

The finite-gate circuit-counting argument gives circuit lower bounds under a fixed finite gate basis. BQP uses bounded error and a family of circuits; a classical indexed-gate description generator is required to prevent advice from encoding uncomputable information.
The quantum PCA discussion explicitly assumes efficient preparation of classical input vectors as states and calls this a strong assumption; it does not infer preparation from the data vector.
The notes develop stabilizer states, Clifford circuits, Gottesman–Knill simulation, magic states and one-way computation, including Pauli measurement updates.
The course surveys error correction and concatenated fault tolerance, but the threshold treatment is succinct and sketch-level rather than a full quantitative gadget/recursion proof.

limitations: The author preface describes the notes as rough and still being polished.

Some Hamiltonian block-encoding/QSVT polynomial approximation results are stated without proof; the sparse block-encoding exercise construction is not a complete local source for every implementation detail.
The threshold chapter is not sufficient by itself for the full QC21 proof obligation.
Preskill Chapter 4 is author-marked incomplete; only its available 70-page file was read.
The typed Preskill Chapter 8 is unavailable; the handwritten 25-page 2011 fault-tolerance note was visually inspected and its exact scope/limits are recorded in qc_r5’s ledger.
qc_r1 reports no second independent complete proof of the general no-broadcasting theorem; the finite-family/singular-state extension remains a local proof obligation.
Source citations document the proposed route but do not certify authored or accepted proofs.
